meta.title: The Life of the Prophet
meta.subtitle: The Life of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ
meta.description: A chronological account of the life of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, from the period before his birth until his death. The content has been prepared primarily on the basis of authentic hadith sources and classical works of prophetic biography; necessary notes have been added on disputed matters or those open to differing reports.

periods.name: The Period Before His Birth
periods.summary: The social and religious structure of pre-Islamic Arabia, Prophet Muhammad's lineage, and the Incident of the Elephant.

periods.name: Birth and Childhood
periods.summary: Prophet Muhammad's birth, his years with his foster mother Halimah, and the deaths of his relatives.

periods.name: Youth and Life Before Prophethood
periods.summary: Trading journeys, Hilf al-Fudul, marriage to Khadijah, and the rebuilding of the Kaaba.

periods.name: The Meccan Period
periods.summary: The beginning of revelation, the first Muslims, the private and public call to Islam, persecution, and the Year of Sorrow.

periods.name: The Hijrah
periods.summary: The journey from Mecca to Medina that marked a turning point in history.

periods.name: Medina — The Early Years
periods.summary: The Prophet's Mosque, the brotherhood between the Muhajirun and the Ansar, the Constitution of Medina, and the Battle of Badr.

periods.name: Medina — Battles and Treaties
periods.summary: The strengthening of Islam through Uhud, the Battle of the Trench, and the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.

periods.name: Expansion, Conquest, and the Final Years
periods.summary: Khaybar, letters to rulers, the Conquest of Mecca, the Farewell Hajj, and his death.

events.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia
events.description:
At the time of Prophet Muhammad's birth, the Arabian Peninsula had a tribal structure and lacked political unity. Most of the peninsula was desert; its main settlements were Mecca, Yathrib, and Taif in the Hijaz. Society was divided into free people, mawali, and slaves; women and girls were not valued, and baby girls were buried alive. Polygamy, blood feuds, interest, and the slave trade were widespread.

Religiously, idol worship was dominant. There were as many as 360 idols in and around the Kaaba; the principal ones were Hubal, Lat, Manat, and Uzza. There were also a small number of Hanifs who believed in one God. Fairs such as Ukaz and Dhu'l-Majaz fostered both commercial and cultural unity. The revolution that Islam would bring to this society takes on meaning against this dark background.
key_lessons: Understanding the background to Islam's call for social justice
What tawhid means in opposition to idol worship
Being alert to remnants of the pre-Islamic age

events.title: The Kaaba and the Rise of Quraysh
events.description:
According to Islamic belief, the Kaaba is the first house of tawhid, built by Prophet Ibrahim and his son Prophet Ismail. The Quraysh tribe became the dominant power in Mecca after taking control of the Kaaba during the time of Qusayy ibn Kilab (around the 5th century). Mecca became a religious and commercial center through Hajj and the fairs.

Quraysh was held in high regard by other tribes because of its guardianship of the Kaaba. This standing would be both an opening and an obstacle for Prophet Muhammad's preaching after he became a prophet.
key_lessons: The historical roots of tawhid
The Abrahamic heritage of the Kaaba
events.reliability_note: Some reports about the origin of the Black Stone have weak chains of transmission.

events.title: Prophet Muhammad's Lineage
events.description:
Prophet Muhammad belonged to the Banu Hashim branch of Quraysh. His father was Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and his mother was Aminah bint Wahb. His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib was one of the most respected figures in Mecca; he is also known for having the well of Zamzam dug again.

Banu Hashim held a special place among the other branches of Quraysh because it undertook the duty of serving pilgrims by providing water and food at the Kaaba (siqayah and rifadah). The distinction of this lineage appears in the tradition of reports, not in the Quran.
key_lessons: How lineage prepared the ground for prophethood
The role of social standing in facilitating the call to Islam

events.title: The Incident of the Elephant
events.description:
Abraha, the Abyssinian (Aksumite) governor of Yemen, had a great cathedral built in Sana'a and tried to draw pilgrims there. When he failed, he set out to destroy the Kaaba with a large army equipped with elephants. As the army approached Mecca, the leading elephant, Mahmud, refused to advance.

As described in Surah al-Fil of the Quran, Allah sent birds called ababil; these birds destroyed the army by pelting it with stones of baked clay (sijjil). Abd al-Muttalib's reply to Abraha is well known: 'I am the owner of the camels; the owner of the Kaaba will protect it.' This event took place shortly before Prophet Muhammad's birth and was regarded in Islamic tradition as a sign of the Prophet's coming.
key_lessons: Allah's protection of His house and His trustworthiness
The fate of arrogance and injustice
Divine power in the face of human power
events.reliability_note: The exact date of the event is disputed: various dates have been given, including 547, 552, 563, 569, 570, and 571. The prevailing view is that it took place approximately 50–55 days before the Prophet's birth. The nature of the ababil birds and precisely what sijjil was are debated.

events.title: The Birth of Prophet Muhammad
events.date_hijri: The Year of the Elephant, Rabi al-Awwal
events.description:
According to the prevailing view, Prophet Muhammad was born in the Banu Hashim quarter of Mecca on a Monday morning, the 12th of Rabi al-Awwal, approximately 50–55 days after the Incident of the Elephant. His father Abdullah had died in Medina (Yathrib) approximately two months before he was born; his estate consisted of five camels, a flock of sheep, and the slave woman Umm Ayman (Barakah).

His grandfather Abd al-Muttalib named him 'Muhammad.' This name was not common among the Arabs at that time. His mother Aminah reported that she named him 'Ahmad.' Although certain things are reported to have happened at his birth, the vast majority of these reports do not have reliable chains of transmission.
key_lessons: The role of being an orphan in shaping his prophetic character
The ground Allah prepared for His prophet
events.reliability_note: The year of birth is disputed: Mahmud Pasha al-Falaki proposed 20 April 571 (9 Rabi al-Awwal), while Muhammad Hamidullah proposed 17 June 569 (12 Rabi al-Awwal). Whether the day was definitely the 12th of Rabi al-Awwal is also disputed; the view that it was the 9th of Rabi al-Awwal is considered stronger.

events.title: With His Foster Mother Halimah
events.description:
According to the custom of the time, children of Mecca were entrusted to wet nurses so that they could grow up in the desert air and learn eloquent Arabic. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was first nursed by his mother, then by Thuwaybah, a bondwoman of Abu Lahab. After that, Halimah bint Abi Dhuayb of the Sa'd ibn Bakr tribe became his wet nurse.

Halimah related that, after she took the young Muhammad into her home, she experienced a period of blessing: the animals produced more milk, and the time of scarcity passed more easily. His foster siblings were Abdullah, Unaysah, and Shayma. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ remained in this setting for about four to five years and learned the eloquent Arabic of the Hawazin there.
key_lessons: The contribution of desert upbringing to language and character
Loyalty: The Prophet honored his wet nurse Halimah until her death

events.title: Shaqq al-Sadr: The Opening of the Chest
events.description:
It is narrated that, while the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was with Halimah, two angels came, opened his chest, washed his heart with Zamzam water, and removed the portion of impurity within it (hakk-ı şeytan). When his foster siblings saw this event and reported it, Halimah became worried and returned the child to his mother Aminah.

Surah ash-Sharh has been interpreted as a metaphorical indication of this event. In Muslim, the hadith of Jibril opening his chest before the Mi'raj is recorded as authentic.
key_lessons: The Prophet's spiritual preparation
Every prophet is prepared in a way specific to his mission
events.reliability_note: The hadith of Shaqq al-Sadr in Muslim concerns the Mi'raj and is authentic. The account of Shaqq al-Sadr during childhood, however, comes through weaker chains of narration. Some scholars regard the use of ash-Sharh 94:1 as evidence for this event as a metaphorical interpretation.

events.title: The Deaths of His Mother and Grandfather
events.description:
When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was six years old, his mother Aminah took him to visit his paternal relatives in Medina. On the return journey, she fell ill and died in the village of Abwa, between Mecca and Medina. After his mother was buried, the child returned to his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib.

He spent two years receiving Abd al-Muttalib's special care and affection, but his grandfather also died when he was eight. On his deathbed, Abd al-Muttalib appointed his son Abu Talib as the child's guardian. Abu Talib and his wife Fatimah bint Asad cared for him, with Fatimah becoming like a second mother to him. The Quran addresses his orphanhood alongside Allah's protection (ad-Duha 93:6).
key_lessons: Patience in orphanhood and Allah's protection
The value of family support

events.title: The Trade Journey to Syria
events.description:
Between the ages of nine and twelve, he joined a trade caravan traveling to Syria (Busra) with his uncle Abu Talib. This journey gave him an opportunity to learn about the Arab world of trade as well as different cultures and religions.

Some sources narrate that he met a Christian monk named Bahira, who lived in a monastery near Busra. It is said that Bahira saw the seal of prophethood on the Prophet's back and advised Abu Talib to protect him and take him back.
key_lessons: The value of learning about different societies
The early foundations of business ethics
events.reliability_note: The account of the meeting with Bahira is not supported by sound chains of narration and is disputed. It should be approached with caution.

events.title: Hilf al-Fudul: The Alliance of the Virtuous
events.description:
After Yemenis defrauded a Meccan merchant, representatives of several tribes gathered at the home of Abdullah ibn Jud'an and swore to protect those who suffered injustice under all circumstances. This agreement was called 'Hilf al-Fudul.'

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who was a young man at the time, also attended this gathering. Years later, after declaring his prophethood, he said: 'I took part in an alliance in the house of Abdullah ibn Jud'an that I would not wish to break even in exchange for red camels. If I were invited to such a society in Islam, I would join it again.' These words show how Islam's universal understanding of justice recognizes even the good values of the Age of Ignorance.
key_lessons: Supporting justice at all times and in all settings
Recognizing good values from before Islam
Standing with the oppressed

events.title: Marriage to Khadijah
events.description:
At the age of 25, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ accepted an offer to manage the trade caravan of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a widowed businesswoman. The offer was influenced by his reputation for honesty and trustworthiness, which had earned him the title 'al-Amin.' After the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned from the journey to Syria with a profit, Khadijah, who admired his character, sent him a marriage proposal through an intermediary; he accepted.

Six children were born from this marriage: Qasim, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and Abdullah (Tayyib/Tahir). Qasim and Abdullah died young. Khadijah was the Prophet's greatest supporter and has the honor of being the first Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ took no other wife during her lifetime and remembered her in the finest terms after her death.
key_lessons: The doors opened by honesty
Spiritual support between spouses
The place of a strong female role model in Islamic history
events.reliability_note: Khadijah's age at the time of her marriage is disputed: the widely reported age is 40, but the report of 28 from Ibn Abbas is more consistent with her having given birth to six children.

events.title: The Rebuilding of the Kaaba and the Black Stone
events.description:
When he was 35, the Kaaba, which had been damaged by flooding and demolished, was rebuilt. A dispute arose among the four major tribes of Mecca over who would place the Black Stone back in position, and swords were nearly drawn; each tribe wanted the honor.

They awaited the decision of the oldest man, who said that the first person to enter should decide. Everyone was pleased when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ entered. His solution was to bring a large cloth, place the stone in its center, and have representatives of the four tribes hold its corners. When the stone was close to its position, he took the Black Stone himself and placed it there. In this way, he prevented a major tribal conflict. This event shows that even before his prophethood, he was the community's natural arbitrator and problem solver.
key_lessons: Reconciliatory leadership
Finding wise solutions
The social importance of arbitration

events.title: The Cave of Hira: The First Revelation
events.date_hijri: The first year of prophethood, Ramadan
events.description:
At the age of 40, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ met Jibril for the first time during Ramadan in the Cave of Hira (Mount Nur), where he often withdrew in seclusion. The angel held him tightly and said three times, 'Read!' Each time, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ replied, 'I cannot read.' Then the first five verses of Surah al-Alaq were revealed: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created!'

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned home frightened, with trembling hands. Khadijah wrapped him up and comforted him, saying, 'Allah will never disgrace you; you are kind to your relatives, speak the truth, and bear the burdens of the weak.' She then took him to her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who said, 'This is the Namus (Jibril) who came to Musa,' and told him that he needed to prepare for a great mission. This moment is the most critical starting point in Islamic history.
key_lessons: The primary place of knowledge and reading in Islam
A spouse's spiritual support
Seeking refuge in Allah in moments of fear and insecurity
events.reliability_note: Sahih (Bukhari and Muslim). Which night of Ramadan it occurred on is disputed; some hold that it was the 17th night, others the 27th.

events.title: The First Muslims
events.description:
The first to believe after the revelation were his wife Khadijah (the first among women), his cousin Ali (the first among children, at about 10 years old), his close friend Abu Bakr (the first among free men), and his freedman Zayd ibn Harithah.

Abu Bakr's acceptance of Islam had a great impact; through him, Uthman, Zubayr, Abdurrahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talhah also became Muslims. These first five to ten people formed the core of the period of private invitation.
key_lessons: The virtue of taking the lead and being first
The influence of one's social circle on embracing Islam
Trust as the foundation of the invitation to Islam
events.reliability_note: Sources classify the first Muslims in different orders. The account here summarizes the distinction commonly used in works on the Prophet's life: the first among women, children, free men, and freed people.

events.title: The Period of Private Invitation
events.description:
For the first three years, the invitation to Islam was carried out privately. The house of al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam (Dar al-Arqam) became the meeting place. The Prophet ﷺ explained Islam one by one to trusted people in his close circle.

This period demonstrates both a cautious strategy and the building of the invitation on personal bonds. The Quran was only beginning to be revealed; although a stir was beginning in society, open conflict had not yet arisen.
key_lessons: The importance of gradual preaching
Inviting others to Islam before establishing a trustworthy setting
The need for each period to have its own strategy

events.title: The Public Invitation: Proclamation on Mount Safa
events.description:
The public invitation began with the verses ash-Shu'ara 214 ('Warn your closest relatives') and al-Hijr 94 ('Proclaim openly what you are commanded'). The Prophet ﷺ climbed Mount Safa, gathered the Quraysh, and asked, 'If I told you that an enemy army was behind this mountain, would you believe me?' When they replied, 'Yes, we have never known you to lie,' he warned them of Allah's punishment.

Abu Lahab angrily departed, saying, 'May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?' Surah al-Lahab was revealed in response to this reaction. The resistance of the Quraysh grew increasingly severe.
key_lessons: The courage to proclaim the truth publicly
How previously earned trust provides a foundation for the invitation
Rejection as one of Allah's established ways

events.title: The Torture of the First Muslims
events.description:
The pressure exerted by the Quraysh was directed particularly at vulnerable and enslaved Muslims. Bilal al-Habashi was tortured under the scorching sun of Makkah with a large stone placed on his chest; Abu Bakr bought him in order to set him free. Ammar ibn Yasir, his mother Sumayyah, and his father Yasir were subjected to severe torture. Sumayyah was martyred by Abu Jahl's spear and became known as the first martyr of Islam.

Whenever Ammar was tortured, the Prophet ﷺ would say to him, 'Be patient, O family of Abu Yasir! Your promised destination is Paradise.' The acceptance of iman by Hamzah and Umar brought the Muslims considerable strength and honor.
key_lessons: Steadfastness and patience in iman
Protecting the vulnerable
The meaning of martyrdom

events.title: The Migration to Abyssinia
events.description:
When the persecution in Makkah became unbearable, the Prophet ﷺ permitted some Muslims to migrate to Abyssinia. The first group consisted of 15 people (11 men and 4 women), while the second consisted of approximately 100 people (82 men and 18 women). Ja'far ibn Abi Talib led the second group.

The envoys of the Quraysh, Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'ah, tried to persuade the Negus to hand the Muslims back. When the Negus opened an inquiry, Ja'far recited verses from Surah Maryam about Isa and his mother; it is narrated that the Negus's eyes filled with tears. The Negus refused to hand them over, and the Muslims remained safe.
key_lessons: The search for a just ruler
The power of dialogue
The Quran's effect on hearts

events.title: The Social and Economic Boycott
events.description:
The Quraysh imposed a comprehensive social and economic boycott on the clans of Hashim and al-Muttalib in order to have the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the Muslims handed over to them. The terms of the boycott were written on a document and hung in the Kaaba: no one was to trade with them, enter into marriage contracts with them, or meet with them.

The Muslims remained confined for approximately three years in a valley called Shi'b Abi Talib. Sources report that, amid hunger and deprivation, they even ate tree leaves. The boycott ended when the consciences of some members of the Quraysh were troubled; it is reported that the document had been destroyed by moths.
key_lessons: Economic pressure endured for the sake of faith
Solidarity within the community
The eventual collapse of oppression under its own weight
events.reliability_note: Reports that the hand of Mansur ibn Ikrimah, who wrote the document, became paralyzed and that the document was destroyed by moths are considered exaggerated.

events.title: The Year of Sorrow: The Deaths of His Uncle and Wife
events.description:
Shortly after the boycott ended, the Prophet ﷺ lost two of his greatest sources of support in succession, causing the year to be named 'Am al-Huzn' (the Year of Sorrow). First, his uncle and protector Abu Talib died without having become a Muslim. Then his wife Khadijah, the first Muslim and his greatest supporter, died at the age of 65.

Khadijah's death coincided with 10 Ramadan; she was buried in the Jannat al-Mu'alla cemetery in Makkah. With these two losses, the Prophet's ﷺ social protection in Makkah weakened considerably, and attacks by the polytheists increased.
key_lessons: The importance of patience and submission in the face of loss
Divine consolation that follows
The value of support from a spouse and family

events.title: The Journey to Ta'if
events.description:
When support in Mecca weakened, the Prophet ﷺ went to Ta'if with his freedman Zayd ibn Harithah. The leaders of the Thaqif tribe humiliated him and turned him away; they also had the rabble stone him. Muhammad ﷺ had to leave Ta'if with his feet bleeding.

On the return journey, a slave named Addas offered him grapes. When the Prophet said the Basmalah, Addas was surprised and asked him about it, and the Prophet told him about himself and the Prophet Jesus. Addas immediately became Muslim. On returning to Mecca, he was able to enter under the protection of Mut'im ibn Adi, who was not yet Muslim. This difficult experience shows the depth of forgiveness and mercy: 'If Allah does not bring forth believers from this generation, He will bring them forth from their descendants.'
key_lessons: Determination to overcome rejection
Mercy: refraining from curses and forgiving
When one door closes, another opens

events.title: The Isra and Mi'raj
events.description:
After the Year of Sorrow, Allah honored His Prophet. A night journey (Isra) took place from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, followed by the Mi'raj, an ascent to the seventh heaven guided by Gabriel. On this journey, Muhammad ﷺ met all the prophets, saw Paradise and Hell, and was addressed by Allah.

The most important outcome was that the five daily prayers were made obligatory. Initially set at 50 prayers, they were reduced to five after Moses advised the Prophet to seek reductions. When the Prophet ﷺ told the people of Mecca about this event in the morning, the Quraysh did not believe him. Abu Bakr, however, said, 'If he said it, it is true,' earning the title 'as-Siddiq.'
key_lessons: The place and importance of salah before Allah
The unity of the prophets and the inclusiveness of Islam
Ease after hardship
events.reliability_note: The date is disputed. The 11th or 12th year before the Hijrah and the 27th of Rajab are commonly cited, but they are not certain. Scholars of Quranic interpretation have debated whether the Isra and Mi'raj took place in body and soul or in a dream; the majority hold that they took place in body and soul.

events.title: The Pledges of Aqabah
events.description:
The First Pledge of Aqabah (621, 12 people): They pledged not to associate partners with Allah, steal, commit adultery, kill children, make false accusations, or oppose what is good. This pledge is also called 'Bey'atü'n-nisâ' (the pledge of women) because it did not include a condition to fight. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was sent to Medina as the first 'mürebbî' to teach Islam.

The Second Pledge of Aqabah (622, 75 people: 73 men + 2 women): This time, an obligation to fight was added; it is known as 'Bey'atü'l-harb.' Twelve nakibs (representatives) were chosen, and As'ad ibn Zurarah became nakîbü'n-nükabâ. This pledge is considered the practical beginning of the Hijrah.
key_lessons: Organization and shared responsibility
The role of a pledge in building a community
The educator's leading role

events.title: The Assassination Plot and the Beginning of the Hijrah
events.description:
The leaders of the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah and decided to kill Muhammad ﷺ. They planned to choose one young man from each tribe to attack him together, so that the blood feud could not be placed on a single tribe.

Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ of this plan through Gabriel. He had Ali lie in his bed, covered him with his green cloak, and left the house while reciting verse 9 of Ya-Sin; the guards at the door could not see him. He met Abu Bakr, and they began the journey of the Hijrah.
key_lessons: Taking precautions and then placing trust in Allah
Ali's self-sacrifice
The powerlessness of human plans against the divine will

events.title: Three Days in the Cave of Thawr
events.description:
The Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr took refuge in a cave on Mount Thawr, south of Mecca, and stayed there for three nights. The Quraysh searchers came as far as the entrance to the cave. When Abu Bakr became worried, the Prophet ﷺ comforted him with verse 40 of at-Tawbah: 'Do not grieve; Allah is with us.'

During this time, Abdullah ibn Abu Bakr brought news during the day, his sister Asma brought food, and Amir ibn Fuhayrah used his flock to cover their tracks. Abdullah ibn Urayqit, who was not yet Muslim but was trustworthy, was hired as a guide.
key_lessons: Complete trust: leaving the outcome to Allah after taking every precaution
A moment that tested friendship and loyalty
Allah's help arriving at the most critical moment
events.reliability_note: The report that a spider spun a web and a dove built a nest at the cave entrance is well known, but its chain of transmission is considered weak. Verse 40 of at-Tawbah is authentic.

events.title: Arrival in Quba and Medina
events.description:
After a journey of approximately 8–9 days, they reached Quba on 8 Rabi al-Awwal. There, the Quba Mosque, regarded as the first mosque in Islam, was built. On Friday, 12 Rabi al-Awwal, the first Friday prayer was performed in the valley of Ranuna, and the historic sermon was delivered.

Upon entering Medina, every tribe competed to host him. The Prophet ﷺ let his camel go freely and said, 'I will stay wherever it kneels.' The camel knelt where the Prophet's Mosque stands today, and he chose Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, the nearest neighbor, as his host. The city of Yathrib now came to be known as 'Medînetü'r-resûl' (the city of the Prophet).
key_lessons: Building a community centered on the mosque
Humility: letting the camel choose instead of a person
Friday as a symbol of a new beginning

events.title: The Construction of the Prophet's Mosque
events.description:
The land where the camel knelt was identified as a place used for drying dates and belonging to two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl; the land was purchased. The Prophet ﷺ personally worked on the construction, carrying stones and saying, 'This load is not the load of Khaybar; our Lord, this is better and purer.'

When the mosque was completed, an educational platform called the Suffah was established beside it. The Companions who stayed there, known as 'Ehlü's-Suffe,' learned and taught knowledge. The Prophet's private rooms were also next to the mosque. The Prophet's Mosque thus served as a center of worship, education, and administration.
key_lessons: Making the mosque the center of life
The intertwining of education and worship
Building the community physically and spiritually together

events.title: Brotherhood Between the Muhajirun and Ansar (Mu'akhah)
events.description:
The Muhajirun who came to Madinah had left their homes, possessions, and loved ones behind. The Prophet ﷺ established a bond of brotherhood between each of them and a member of the Ansar. At first, this bond was so deep that it even included inheritance rights.

The selflessness (ithar) of the Ansar is praised in the Quran: 'They give their brothers preference over themselves, even when they are in need.' A famous example is Sa'd b. Rabi', who offered his brother Abdurrahman b. Awf his home and half his wealth. Abdurrahman b. Awf, however, only wanted to know where the marketplace was.
key_lessons: True brotherhood is based on sacrifice
There can be no social integration without economic integration
The virtue of selflessness (ithar)

events.title: The Constitution of Madinah
events.description:
The Prophet ﷺ made a comprehensive agreement between the Muslims of Madinah (the Muhajirun and the Ansar) and various Jewish tribes. Known in history as the 'Document of Madinah' or the 'First Islamic Constitution,' this document contained the following fundamental principles: the formation of a single ummah by different groups, recognition of freedom of religion, an obligation of mutual defense, and referral of disputes to the Prophet ﷺ.

The text has been preserved through Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham's al-Sirah and in Abu Ubayd's Kitab al-Amwal. This document reflects an approach to pluralistic governance that had no equal anywhere in the world at the time.
key_lessons: Governance of a pluralistic society
The importance of written law and agreements
Peaceful coexistence among different groups
events.reliability_note: The number of articles is disputed: Wellhausen classified the document as having 47 articles, Hamidullah 52, Lecker 64, and Serjeant 70. The major Jewish tribes are mentioned in the text as allies of Arab tribes, rather than by name.

events.title: The Establishment of the Adhan
events.description:
The Muslims discussed how to call people to salah; suggestions such as a bell, a horn, and a fire were rejected. During this time, Abdullah b. Zayd al-Ansari learned the words of the adhan in a dream. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'This is a true dream,' and instructed him to teach it to Bilal. Bilal al-Habashi became the first muezzin.

Umar had seen the same dream, but Abdullah acted first. When the adhan was first called at the Prophet's Mosque, there was great excitement in Madinah. Bilal continued in this role throughout his life, with his powerful voice that carried over long distances.
key_lessons: Consultation and collective decision-making
A dream gaining religious legitimacy under suitable conditions
The most honorable duty given to someone who appears weak
events.reliability_note: 1 or 2 AH. It is not found in Bukhari or Muslim; it appears in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi. Although its chain of transmission is disputed, it has been accepted by the majority of scholars.

events.title: The Qiblah Turns Toward the Ka'bah
events.description:
For approximately 16–17 months after the arrival in Madinah, salah was performed facing al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ wished for the qiblah to be turned toward the Ka'bah during this period; his looking toward the sky was answered in al-Baqarah 144: 'We see you turning your face toward the sky; We will turn you toward a qiblah that will please you.'

The change of qiblah took place in the middle of salah; this demonstrated both the flexibility of worship and the importance of immediate obedience to Allah's command. Al-Baqarah 143 describes this change as a 'test of true faith.'
key_lessons: Immediate obedience to a command
A test does not exclude the believer
Reestablishing the connection with the Abrahamic heritage

events.title: The Battle of Badr
events.description:
The first major battle in Islamic history. The expedition, initially undertaken to intercept Abu Sufyan's trade caravan, turned into a major battle when the Quraysh sent an army of 1,000. The Muslims numbered approximately 305–313. That night, the Prophet ﷺ prayed with all his heart: 'O Lord! If You destroy this group today, no one will remain on earth to worship You.'

In the battle, 70 leading figures of the Quraysh, including Abu Jahl, were killed, and 70 people were taken captive; 14 Muslims were martyred. The captives were offered the option of paying a ransom or teaching 10 Muslims to read and write (as narrated by Ibn Hisham). The Quran states that angels provided assistance in this battle.
key_lessons: Trusting in iman when outnumbered
Supplication as an important part of battle
Humane treatment of captives and education as ransom
The importance of taking a strategic position
events.reliability_note: Authentic. The number of Muslims is given as 305 or 313; the latter is more common.

events.title: The Battle of Uhud
events.description:
The Quraysh came with an army of approximately 3,000 to avenge Badr. The Muslims numbered approximately 700; moreover, Abdullah b. Ubayy left the battlefield with 300 hypocrites. At first, the Muslims had the upper hand.

The Prophet ﷺ had given the archers strict orders: 'Whatever happens, do not leave your positions.' Seeing that the Muslims had gained the upper hand, most of the archers left their positions to collect spoils. Khalid b. Walid took advantage of this opening and attacked from behind, turning the situation around. Approximately 70 Companions, including Hamzah, were martyred. The Prophet's ﷺ tooth was broken and his face was wounded, but he did not fall into enemy hands.
key_lessons: Absolute obedience to the commander's orders
Greed for spoils leading to disaster
Learning from defeat and not giving up
Battle as a test of iman

events.title: The Exile of Banu Nadir
events.description:
The Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir, who violated the Document of Madinah and attempted an assassination, were forced to settle in Khaybar after the Prophet ﷺ expelled them from Madinah. The property and lands they left behind were distributed among the Muslims.

Surah al-Hashr recounts this event; it also addresses the hypocrites' failure to keep their promises: 'We will never abandon you; we will help you.'
key_lessons: Those who betray an agreement will be held accountable
Allah's help comes in unexpected ways

events.title: The Battle of the Trench (the Battle of al-Ahzab)
events.description:
A large coalition (ahzab) of Arab tribes and Jewish groups, led by the Quraysh, besieged Madinah. At the suggestion of the Persian Companion Salman al-Farisi, a trench was dug on the northern side of the city. This strategy had never been seen before in the Arab tradition of warfare.

During the siege, which lasted approximately 20–27 days, the enemy could not cross the trench. Drought, famine, and cold placed the Muslims in a difficult situation; Surah al-Ahzab describes the fear and hardship of those days. In the end, Allah thwarted the enemy armies and scattered them with the wind.
key_lessons: Strategy and consultation: Salman's idea
Enduring together in unity
Innovative methods of defense
events.reliability_note: The date was 5 Shawwal / March 627 CE; different reports give the duration of the siege as 20 to 27 days.

events.title: The Banu Qurayzah Affair
events.description:
During the siege of the Trench, the Jewish tribe of Banu Qurayzah violated the Charter of Medina, attempted to strike the Muslims from behind, and cooperated with the enemy. After the siege of the Trench was lifted, Banu Qurayzah were besieged for 25 days and surrendered.

The fate of the tribe was decided by the arbitrator they had chosen, Sa'd ibn Mu'adh; Sa'd was then on his deathbed from a wound dating back to Uhud. His judgment corresponded to the ruling applied in the Torah to tribes that committed treachery.
key_lessons: The heavy price of betraying a treaty
Accepting the decision of one's chosen arbitrator
events.reliability_note: Reports put the number of warriors killed between 400 and 900. Modern historians suggest that this figure may have been exaggerated.

events.title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
events.description:
The Prophet ﷺ set out with approximately 1,400–1,500 Companions to perform Umrah; the Quraysh prevented them from entering Mecca. After lengthy negotiations, the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed with Suhayl ibn Amr. Its terms were: they would return without performing Umrah that year and perform a three-day Umrah the following year; there would be no fighting for 10 years; anyone who fled from Mecca to Medina would be returned, but anyone who fled from Medina to Mecca would not be returned; and tribes could ally with whichever side they wished.

Some Companions considered these terms unfavorable; even Umar objected. In time, however, it became clear that the treaty had opened the door to a great opportunity: the number of people who embraced Islam in the following two years exceeded the total for the previous 18 years. The Quran described this treaty as 'a clear victory.'
key_lessons: What appears to be a short-term loss may become a long-term gain
Peace can be a more powerful tool than war
The Prophet's foresight
events.reliability_note: Reports put the number of Companions who pledged allegiance between 700 and 1,600; 1,400–1,500 is widely accepted.

events.title: The Conquest of Khaybar
events.description:
Khaybar, 150 km from Medina, was where Banu Nadir had settled after betraying the Charter of Medina, and it had become a center of incitement against the Muslims. The Prophet ﷺ set out on an expedition with a force of approximately 1,600; the fortresses were conquered one by one.

Ali's conquest of the fortress of Qamus is well known; according to a report, he tore off its gate and used it as a shield. The land was left in Jewish hands to cultivate for a time in return for half of its produce. This arrangement continued after the death of the Prophet ﷺ until the time of Umar. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the Muslims returning from Abyssinia also shared in the joy of this conquest.
key_lessons: Preventing security threats at their source
Humane treatment of the people of conquered lands
events.reliability_note: The numbers of warriors may have been exaggerated in some sources. The incident of poisoned meat, in which Bishr ibn al-Bara died, is reported with a strong chain of transmission.

events.title: Letters of Invitation to Rulers
events.description:
After Hudaybiyyah, letters of invitation bearing the seal 'Muhammad Rasulullah' were sent to neighboring rulers. Dihyah al-Kalbi was sent as an envoy to the Byzantine Emperor Heraclius; Heraclius treated the letter with respect, but there is no definitive evidence that he embraced Islam. The Sasanian Khosrow Parviz tore up the letter; the Muqawqis of Egypt did not embrace Islam, but sent gifts, among them Mariyah al-Qibtiyyah. There are strong reports that Ashamah, the Negus of Abyssinia, accepted Islam.

These letters were among the clearest steps demonstrating that Islam is a universal call that transcends tribal boundaries.
key_lessons: The universal message of Islam
The legitimacy of conveying the message through diplomacy
Different responses did not render the Prophet's letter meaningless
events.reliability_note: The account that a letter was sent to Heraclius and that he met Abu Sufyan appears in authentic sources. However, the various copies of the letters and some historical details may differ between reports.

events.title: The Battle of Mu'tah
events.description:
Harith ibn Umayr, the envoy whom the Prophet ﷺ sent to Busra, was killed by a Ghassanid ruler. Following this violation of an envoy's immunity, an army of 3,000 was dispatched to Mu'tah; this was the first armed encounter with the Christian Byzantines and Ghassanids.

After three commanders were martyred in succession, Khalid ibn al-Walid took command and successfully withdrew the army. That day in Medina, the Prophet ﷺ described the commanders' martyrdom as though he could see it; he gave Khalid the title 'Sayfullah' (the Sword of Allah).
key_lessons: The immunity of envoys and diplomats
Continuity and flexibility of command
Merit: a well-executed retreat is also a success

events.title: The Make-up Umrah
events.description:
As required by the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Muslims visited the Ka'bah the following year. The Prophet ﷺ and approximately 2,000 Muslims entered Mecca; the Quraysh vacated the city. During the three-day visit, they performed tawaf around the Ka'bah and sa'y.

Bilal al-Habashi called the adhan from atop the Ka'bah; for Bilal, who had been degraded as a slave for years, this was one of the greatest moments in history. The Quraysh had effectively recognized the Muslims' right to worship at the Ka'bah.
key_lessons: Keeping one's word
A quiet declaration of Islam's growing strength

events.title: The Conquest of Mecca
events.description:
The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was broken when Banu Bakr, an ally of the Quraysh, attacked Khuza'ah. The Prophet ﷺ made preparations in secret and set out with an army of 10,000. Abu Sufyan was captured while scouting around Medina; he embraced Islam through the mediation of Abbas.

The army entered Mecca from four directions under the order: 'Do not use the sword unless you are attacked.' The city was conquered almost without bloodshed. At the Ka'bah, the Prophet ﷺ declared a general amnesty with words recalling what Yusuf had said to his brothers: 'Go, you are all free.' The 360 idols in the Ka'bah were broken as the words 'Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished' (al-Isra 81) were recited. Bilal called the adhan from the roof of the Ka'bah.
key_lessons: The power of forgiveness to win hearts
The triumph of tawhid: the breaking of the idols
Revival, not revenge

events.title: The Battle of Hunayn and the Siege of Ta'if
events.description:
Approximately 17 days after the conquest of Mecca, the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes ambushed the Muslim army of 12,000. Confident in its superior numbers, the army initially panicked (at-Tawbah 25); the Prophet ﷺ did not retreat. When Abbas called out loudly, 'O people of Aqabah!', the Companions gathered, and victory was won.

The fleeing enemy took refuge in Ta'if. The Muslims besieged the fortress, using a catapult for the first time, but could not capture it; the siege was lifted. About a year later, the people of Ta'if embraced Islam of their own accord.
key_lessons: The danger of relying on numbers and strength
True strength lies in Allah's help
Patience: Ta'if eventually came around

events.title: The Expedition of Tabuk
events.description:
Upon hearing that the Byzantines were preparing a major campaign, the Muslims set out for Tabuk with an army of approximately 30,000 called 'Ceyşü'l-Usre' (the Army of Hardship). The hardship of the expedition was reflected in the financial sacrifices made: Abu Bakr donated all his wealth, Umar half of his, and Uthman provided for one third of the army.

The Byzantines signed non-aggression agreements, and no battle took place. However, this expedition exposed the hypocrites; those who stayed behind without an excuse were exposed in the Qur'an without being named. It was the last major military expedition in which the Prophet ﷺ participated.
key_lessons: The measure of sacrifice
Hypocrites revealing themselves in times of hardship
Acting out of faith in one's duty, rather than confidence in strength

events.title: The Arabian Peninsula Embraces Islam
events.description:
After the expedition of Tabuk, Arab tribes sent delegations one after another and embraced Islam. This year was called 'Senetü'l-Vüfûd' (the Year of Delegations). Thaqif, Banu Tamim, Banu Hanifah, and other major tribes sent envoys to Medina.

Surah an-Nasr addresses these developments with the words: 'When Allah's help comes and the conquest is achieved, you see people entering Allah's religion in crowds.' After this surah was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ frequently glorified Allah and sought His forgiveness; those around him interpreted this as a sign that the end of his life was near.
key_lessons: The message bears fruit over time
Victory should be an occasion for praise, not ingratitude

events.title: The Farewell Hajj and Farewell Sermon
events.description:
The Prophet's ﷺ first and last Hajj. Approximately 100,000 to 124,000 Muslims took part in this Hajj. The sermon delivered at Jabal al-Rahmah in Arafat is one of the most comprehensive declarations in Islamic history.

The main principles of the sermon: the inviolability of life, property, and honor; the abolition of interest from the pre-Islamic period; the end of blood feuds from the pre-Islamic period; good treatment of women; individual responsibility for wrongdoing (no one bears another person's sin); the brotherhood of Muslims; and the rejection of superiority based on race or color (superiority lies only in piety). After the sermon, al-Ma'idah 3 was revealed: 'Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favor upon you, and chosen Islam as your religion.'
key_lessons: Islam's approach to human rights
Equality: differences in color, race, and language are not grounds for superiority
The completion of the religion and increased responsibility
events.reliability_note: The text of the sermon appears in different narrations; the version compiled in al-Jahiz's el-Beyân ve't-tebyîn combines separate addresses delivered at Arafat, Mina, and Aqabah.

events.title: The Army of Usamah ibn Zayd
events.description:
During his final illness, the Prophet ﷺ appointed Usamah ibn Zayd as commander of an expedition toward Syria; Usamah was only 18–20 years old. Some Companions objected to the young commander; the Prophet ﷺ responded firmly: 'You also objected to his father's command; he was fit to command, and so is this one.'

The expedition was postponed by the Prophet's ﷺ death, but Abu Bakr resolutely sent it off. This event shows both appointment based on merit and loyalty to the Prophet's wishes.
key_lessons: Merit: ability, not age
Loyalty to final wishes
Trust in the Prophet's decision

events.title: The Death of the Prophet ﷺ
events.description:
About three months after the Farewell Hajj, the Prophet ﷺ fell ill. He spent his final days in Aishah's room; during his illness, Abu Bakr led the prayers. Shortly before his death, he came out to the mosque, looked at the congregation, and smiled; this was the last time he was seen.

On Monday before noon, he breathed his last in Aishah's arms. Among his final words were 'er-Refîku'l-A'lâ' (I wish to be with the Most Exalted Companion) and 'Prayer and those under your care (the weak).' He lived approximately 63 solar years and approximately 63 lunar years.
key_lessons: The Prophet's humanity and mortality
Islam is bound to Allah, not to a person
Even death carries a message
events.reliability_note: The date of his death is agreed to be 12 Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH / 8 June 632 CE; some sources say 13 Rabi al-Awwal.

events.title: Abu Bakr's Historic Speech
events.description:
After news of the death, Umar could not believe it and said, 'He has not died as the hypocrites claim; he has gone to his Lord and will return like Musa.' Abu Bakr came to the mosque, uncovered the Prophet's ﷺ face, kissed his forehead, and said: 'May my mother and father be sacrificed for you; you are beautiful in life and in death.'

He then ascended the pulpit and spoke these historic words: 'Whoever worships Muhammad, let them know that Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah, let them know that Allah is alive and does not die.' When he recited Aal Imran 144, everyone, including Umar, began to weep.
key_lessons: Faith directed toward Allah, not a person
A leader remaining calm and clear in the hardest moment
The Qur'an's power to guide life directly
